To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the NAVA level can be daily adjusted to the maximal diaphrammatic electrical activity during spontaneous breathing trial, with a goal of 60% of the maximal electrical activity.

daily titration with a goal of 60% of the maximum diaphragmatic electrical activation during a spontaneous breathing test was feasible and well-tolerated, and that this approach resulted in an increase of the diaphragmatic electrical output and a decrease of the pressure delivered, while preserving ventilation and oxygenation.
the NAVA level can be adjusted daily in relation to the EAdimax measured during an SBT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of a method of ventilator control for use with a patient-ventilator system.
the development of a method to determine the NAVA level in a way that is independent of the ventilator.
the study of the effects of the daily adjustment of NAVA level on respiratory mechanics and respiratory drive.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the daily titration of neururally adjusted ventilatory assist level in relation to diaphragmatic electrical activation is feasible and well-tolerated and allows to decrease pressure delivered while preserving breathing, alveolar ventilation and oxygenation until extubation.
NAVA is a safe and feasible weaning mode that can be used as a first-line weaning mode.
the NAVA mode of ventilation is a promising tool for the weaning process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NAVA level should be titrated daily with an electrical goal to obtain a 50–60% EAdi during an SBT.
NAVA can improve the weaning process by allowing a reduction in ventilatory support, which may be associated with a reduction in the duration of mechanical ventilation.
the use of the EAdi to titrate NAVA in the weaning process is a feasible and promising approach.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NAVA can be used to wean patients off mechanical ventilation.
the electrical activity of the diaphragm is the most important factor to consider when titrating NAVA in the ICU.
daily titration with electrical goals may be a promising strategy for weaning with NAVA.
